segments.text: We spend a lot of time trying to predict the future, but no matter how carefully we plan,
we all share a massive blind spot when it comes to anticipating how people will actually behave.
To understand why forecasting is so difficult, look at Hanoi in 1902. The city faced a very modern
problem. Their newly constructed sewer system had become a superhighway for rats. The authorities
devised a plan that looked flawless on paper. They instituted a bounty system, paying citizens
for every severed rat tail they turned in. At first, the results were staggering. Tails poured
in by the thousands, proving to the planners that their incentive structure was working exactly as
designed. But counting severed tails created an illusion of success. The planners were looking
at the metrics on their desks, completely missing what was happening out on the streets.
Soon, people started noticing a bizarre anomaly. Living rats were running around the city,
entirely missing their tails. The system's designers missed a simple biological reality.
Rats can live full act of lives without a tail, and crucially, they can keep having more rats.
The rat hunters realized they could maximize their profits with a small adjustment. They caught
the rats, clipped the tails for the bounty, and then released the rodents back into the sewers.
A dead rat pays once. A live rat pays forever. Some entrepreneurial citizens took this logic
even further. Rather than hunting in the sewers, they started literal rat farms to harvest tails
continuously. The government paid out thousands of bounties, but the city ended up with more rats
than when they started. The financial incentive designed to eliminate the pests actually encouraged
the population to keep them alive. The Hanoi rat bounty highlights a persistent gap between
expert design and actual human adaptation. This graphic shows what creators intended alongside
what users actually did. Compare what people expected with what happened next. In 1995, Clifford
stole doubted online shopping could compete with malls. Yet buying online quickly became a daily
habit. In 1940, Henry Ford predicted a flying car was imminent. Decades later, people still make
their everyday trips bound to the road. SMS was built strictly to send short technical messages
over mobile networks. Its creators did not expect young users to hijack the tool and turn texting
into a primary way to stay in touch. And Australia imported cane toads to eat beetles that were
destroying sugar cane. The toads barely touched the pests. Instead, they aggressively poisoned
native wildlife and spread uncontrollably across the country. Whether you are dealing with technology,
ecology, or economics, user behavior and biological reality consistently override the original blueprint.
That same unpredictability applies directly to the rollout of artificial intelligence.
What might people actually do with AI that neither the optimists nor the warriors are predicting?
The most important thing AI does in your lifetime, good or bad, is likely something
nobody in any lab or think tank has thought of yet. That lack of clear foresight is not a reason
to fear the future. It is a mandate to walk into it with your eyes open. You do not need to predict
the future perfectly. You simply need to recognize uncertainty and watch how everyday people actually
use these tools. By observing reality instead of clinging to forecasts, you can build adaptable
skills that remain valuable even when the technological landscape shifts. Some of the biggest
results are the ones nobody predicted. That's the best reason to stay curious.
